name: The Bradyarrhythmias: Disorders of the Atrioventricular Node
aliases: Bradyarrhythmia due to AV node disease

clinicalPearls: The AV node is specialized for slow conduction, creating a delay between atrial and ventricular activation and acting as the electrical gatekeeper to the ventricle; its intrinsic backup pacemaker (escape) rate is roughly 20-60 beats/min, normally overridden by the faster sinus node (60-100 beats/min).
First-degree AV block means every atrial impulse still conducts but with an abnormally prolonged PR interval (>200 ms); the term block is a misnomer since conduction is delayed, not interrupted.

Mobitz I (Wenckebach) second-degree block shows progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat with grouped beating and progressive RR shortening; it is typically within the AV node, hemodynamically stable, and usually does not warrant pacing when asymptomatic.

Mobitz II second-degree block shows a fixed PR interval before a dropped beat, is usually infranodal with a wider QRS, carries a risk of sudden death from an unreliable escape rhythm, and warrants permanent pacing even without symptoms.
In 2:1 AV block the ECG cannot reliably distinguish type I from type II; a PR <160 ms with a wide QRS before the conducted beat favors infranodal (type II) block.

QRS width of the escape rhythm localizes the block: a narrow QRS escape implies block in the AV node or proximal His with a faster, more stable junctional rhythm, whereas a wide QRS escape (without preexisting bundle branch block) implies distal His or bundle branch block and a slower, less reliable rhythm.

Vagal maneuvers and carotid sinus massage slow AV nodal conduction but may paradoxically improve infranodal conduction, while atropine, isoproterenol, and exercise improve AV nodal conduction but may worsen infranodal conduction - useful for localizing the level of block.

On the His bundle electrogram, the AH interval (AV nodal conduction) is normally <130 ms and the HV interval (His-Purkinje conduction) is normally <=55 ms; a markedly prolonged HV interval predicts progression to higher-grade block.
Functional causes of AV block (autonomic, metabolic/endocrine, drug-related) tend to be reversible, whereas most structural causes producing fibrosis are permanent.
Congenital complete heart block with a narrow QRS typically increases heart rate with exercise, whereas acquired complete heart block (especially wide QRS) does not respond to exercise.

Acquired persistent AV conduction failure is rare in healthy adults (estimated incidence about 1 per 5000 per year in the U.S.), but becomes much more common with ischemia, aging/fibrosis, or infiltrative disease.

Idiopathic progressive fibrosis/sclerosis of the conduction system is the most common acquired cause, accounting for roughly 50% of AV block; it often begins in the fourth decade and is accelerated by atherosclerosis, hypertension, and diabetes.
harrison.pathophysiology: AV nodal myocytes sit at a relatively high resting membrane potential (~-60 mV), exhibit slow phase-0 upstrokes mediated by L-type calcium current (with a relative lack of fast sodium current), and show spontaneous phase-4 depolarization, conferring backup automaticity. Weak electrical coupling from sparse gap junctions (predominantly connexin-40) plus increased extracellular volume slows conduction and protects the ventricle. The AV junction comprises a transitional (atrionodal) cell zone showing decremental conduction, the compact node, and the penetrating His bundle; conduction continues through the His, right and left bundle branches, and the fast-conducting Purkinje network (1-3 m/s). Bradycardia and block arise when conduction across this axis is compromised by fibrosis/sclerosis, calcification (Lev, Lenegre disease), ischemia/infarction, infiltrative or inflammatory disease, drugs, heightened vagal tone, or congenital/genetic abnormalities; consequences range from fatigue and syncope to asystolic death if no reliable escape emerges. Functional (autonomic/metabolic/drug) causes are often reversible while structural fibrosis is typically permanent.
additionalDifferentials: Sinus node dysfunction / sinus bradycardia (sick sinus syndrome) as a competing cause of symptomatic bradycardia
Drug effect (beta blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin) producing reversible AV conduction slowing
Heightened vagal tone (sleep, well-conditioned athletes, carotid sinus hypersensitivity, vasovagal/cough/micturition syncope)
Congenital complete heart block (e.g., maternal lupus)
infectionMimics: Lyme carditis (Borrelia burgdorferi) - a common infectious cause of AV block, typically AV-nodal with narrow junctional escape >40 beats/min, usually improving within about a week of antibiotic therapy
Infective endocarditis with perivalvular abscess - AV block here should prompt urgent surgical consultation
nonInfectiousMimics: Senile degenerative fibrosis/calcification of the conduction system (Lev disease)
Lenegre disease (sclerodegenerative distal bundle branch disease in younger patients)
Aortic (and less commonly mitral) valve annular calcification encroaching on the conduction system
Autoimmune/rheumatologic disease (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, mixed connective tissue disease, scleroderma)
Neuromuscular disease (myotonic dystrophy, Kearns-Sayre syndrome, muscular dystrophies)
Iatrogenic injury (valve/cardiac surgery, TAVR, septal myectomy/alcohol septal ablation, catheter ablation)
Hereditary progressive familial heart block (e.g., SCN5A mutations) and lamin A/C cardiomyopathy
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG to classify the degree and pattern of block and assess QRS width/escape rhythm
Transthoracic echocardiography to assess for structural/valvular disease, ejection fraction, and wall motion
Advanced imaging (cardiac MRI, CT, FDG-PET, technetium pyrophosphate scanning) for infiltrative disease, especially when block develops at age <=60 years
Ambulatory/continuous ECG monitoring to correlate symptoms with bradyarrhythmia
Provocative testing - vagal maneuvers, carotid sinus massage, exercise, atropine, isoproterenol - to localize the level of block
Invasive electrophysiologic study with His bundle electrogram (AH and HV interval measurement) in syncope with suspected high-grade or infranodal block
Evaluation for ischemia when clinical suspicion is present
redFlags: Wide-complex escape rhythm at a slow rate (e.g., ~30 beats/min) implying infranodal block and an unreliable escape
Mobitz II second-degree or complete (third-degree) heart block
Syncope or presyncope attributable to bradycardia
Markedly prolonged HV interval (>100 ms carries an annual incidence of complete AV block approaching 10%)
High-grade AV block complicating anterior MI (distal block, wide unstable escape, high mortality)
New AV block with infective endocarditis suggesting perivalvular abscess
Alternating bundle branch block or bifascicular/trifascicular block with intermittent third-degree block
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on the level of block. AV-nodal (proximal) block - including Mobitz I and most inferior-MI-related block - tends to have a faster, stable narrow-complex escape and is often reversible with a favorable outcome. Infranodal (distal His-Purkinje) block, Mobitz II, and high-grade block in anterior MI carry unstable wide-complex escape rhythms, higher mortality, and a risk of sudden asystolic death, so pacing is indicated even when asymptomatic. Functional/reversible causes generally resolve; structural fibrotic disease is usually permanent and progressive.
pitfalls: Mislabeling 2:1 AV block as type I when it may be infranodal type II - the surface ECG cannot reliably distinguish them
Assuming all AV block is benign vagal phenomenon and missing serious infranodal disease that warrants pacing despite absent symptoms
Overlooking reversible/treatable causes (offending drugs, electrolyte derangement, ischemia, hypothyroidism, sleep apnea, Lyme carditis) before committing to permanent therapy
Failing to pursue advanced imaging for infiltrative disease (e.g., sarcoidosis) when AV block presents at a younger age (<=60 years)
Misinterpreting Mobitz I at very short paced cycle lengths as pathologic - it can be a normal physiologic response; it is abnormal at cycle lengths >500 ms (<120 beats/min) without high vagal tone
Not recognizing that a new perivalvular abscess in endocarditis can present as AV block requiring urgent surgery
harrison.severityClassification: Electrocardiographic grading: First-degree AV block - all atrial impulses conduct but PR is prolonged (>200 ms), delay usually within the AV node. Second-degree AV block - intermittent failure of AV conduction; Type I/Mobitz I/Wenckebach (progressive PR prolongation until a dropped beat, usually AV-nodal) and Type II/Mobitz II (fixed PR before a dropped beat, usually infranodal, often with wide QRS). Third-degree (complete) AV block - complete AV dissociation with a ventricular (escape) rate slower than the atrial rate.
management: Identify and reverse treatable causes first — withdraw AV-nodal blocking agents (beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, digoxin), treat ischaemia, correct electrolyte disturbance and hypothyroidism, and treat Lyme carditis or infiltrative disease
For acute symptomatic bradycardia give atropine and, if inadequate, a chronotrope such as isoprenaline while arranging temporary transcutaneous or transvenous pacing
Implant a permanent pacemaker for symptomatic AV block, and for Mobitz II or high-grade/complete infranodal block even when asymptomatic given the unreliable escape rhythm
Observe asymptomatic first-degree and Mobitz I (Wenckebach) block, which are usually nodal and stable and do not require pacing
Consider conduction-system (His-bundle or left-bundle-branch) pacing or biventricular pacing where a high ventricular-pacing burden or impaired function is anticipated
Investigate for underlying structural or infiltrative disease with echocardiography and advanced imaging, particularly when block occurs in younger patients
Refer to electrophysiology for device implantation and for His-bundle electrogram assessment in unexplained syncope with suspected infranodal block
